newsitem.title: SPAIN: IATA airlines attack high infrastructure charges.
newsitem.headline: IATA airlines attack high infrastructure charges.

text.p: European airlines are alarmed at the prospect of further steady increases in the charges they pay for air traffic control, airline representatives said at an International Air Transport Association (IATA) conference on Wednesday.

Infrastructure costs (which include en-route air traffic control, approach and landing charges) in Europe rose by an average 7.2 percent a year between 1985 and 1994, said Fritz Otti, chief financial officer for Austrian Airlines.
Austrian Airlines itself had seen air traffic management costs increase to 6.7 percent from 4.7 percent of total revenues in the last four or five years, he said.
"That knocks out a five or six percent dividend to our shareholders," he added.

What worries IATA member airlines more is the prospect of further sharp rises in future to fund the cost of developing the harmonised air traffic control and management system that Europe will need by early next century to cope with increasing congestion.
"User charges have been rising at seven or eight percent a year and will continue to do so," said Tony Kelly, IATA director of industry monetary affairs.

"That's bad news for the airlines because these are costs we cannot control and many of the people imposing these are agencies of governments -- the same governments which are telling airlines they must reduce their fares," Kelly told Reuters during the two-day conference.

IATA estimates its members' en-route charges on international flights (domestic flight charges are cheaper) amount to 10 percent of operating costs, or around $11 billion in 1995, rising to nearer $12 billion this year.
"One airline told me it lost 50 percent of an excursion fare on infrastructure charges," Kelly said.

The European Air Traffic Control Harmonisation and Integration Project (EATCHIP), managed by Eurocontrol, aims to harmonise the air traffic systems of 33 European states by 1998 and integrate them early in the 21st century.
But it could not say exactly how much this would cost, EATCHIP chairman Tony Goldman said.
Research and development in Europe into air traffic management systems now cost 200 million Ecus a year, he said.
"I believe this will have to be maintained for the next few years. The European Union contributes...and airlines will inevitably have to contribute," he told the conference.

Much of the conference was devoted to discussing methods of paying for the future European Air Traffic Management System through a mixture of European Union funding, private financing and government lending to ease the burden on the end users -- the airlines.
High user charges put European airlines at a competitive disadvantage to carriers from the U.S. where charges are lower, airlines said.
They were adamant the current rate of increase in charges could not go on.
Intra-European fares fell around 20 percent between 1984 and 1995, said Scandinavian Airlines System's director of governmental charges Anders Sviden.
"In the same period the costs for en-route charges has also in real terms increased by about 75 percent. These trends can of course not continue."
